transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I suppose what finally got me to make the appointment is that my concentration has become unreliable, and that’s not really like me. I’m a dentist, so I’m used to being very focused and precise, and lately I’ll be reviewing a patient chart at the clinic and realize I’ve read the same line two or three times without taking it in.

And it’s not just at work. I paint watercolors, and even when I’m trying to lay out a wash—something that usually settles me—I’ll suddenly notice my mind has drifted off into all the things that could go wrong. Not one specific thing, necessarily, just… a whole chain of possibilities. Then I have to pull myself back and start over. It’s frustrating, and honestly a little unsettling, because I rely on being able to keep my mind where I put it.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a number of different things in your life, like work, health, or other responsibilities, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?

Yes, I do. It’s not usually one single crisis in front of me, which almost makes it harder to explain. My mind just keeps circling around all sorts of things.

I worry about whether my older patients are being properly looked after now that I’m stepping back, even though logically I know there are capable people involved. Then I’ll start thinking about the handoff of the practice—whether the financial side of it is sound, whether I’ve missed some detail, whether something will come back to bite me later. And then it shifts again to what I’ll be once I’m fully retired… whether I’ll become useless, or sort of fade into the background.

And I can hear myself saying it and think, “This is out of proportion.” It’s not as if there’s an immediate disaster happening. But once the thought starts, it keeps going around and around.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed feeling down, depressed, or losing interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy, like your painting or other activities?

I’m not sure I’d call it “depressed,” exactly. I don’t think I’ve been walking around feeling sad in that heavy way, if that’s what you mean. It’s more that I get… preoccupied, and then things don’t feel as easy to settle into.

With painting, for example, I still want to do it. I still like the idea of it, and I’ll set everything out — the paper, the brushes, the little porcelain palette I use — but sometimes I don’t get that same smooth absorption in it because my mind wanders off. So I wouldn’t say I’ve lost interest in it. It’s just harder to stay with it long enough to enjoy it properly.

So, no, I haven’t really noticed feeling down most of the time or losing pleasure in things across the board. It’s more like I’m distracted from them.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms, like restlessness, muscle tension, or trouble sleeping, that seem to go along with these worried thoughts?

Yes, the sleep part has definitely been noticeable. Most nights I’ll get into bed genuinely tired — not just “I should sleep now,” but physically ready to be asleep — and then as soon as the house is quiet, it’s like my mind takes that as permission to start going through everything.

I’ll find myself replaying patient transfers, thinking, “Did I make that clear enough? Did I leave anything for someone else to misunderstand?” And then it moves into the money side of things, little details around the practice and retirement, and I’ll go over them again and again as if I’m going to solve something at 11:30 at night, which of course I’m not.

And even when I do fall asleep, it doesn’t feel very restorative. I’m often awake at four or five in the morning, and it’s not that I feel rested and ready to get up. It’s more like I never fully settled in the first place. The night feels broken up, or shallow somehow. Then I start the day already a bit worn down, which doesn’t help.

Have you ever experienced sudden episodes where you feel intense fear or discomfort that comes on quickly, like a panic attack, where you might feel your heart racing, short of breath, or even fear losing control?

No, I don’t think so — not in the way you’re describing. I mean, I’ve certainly had moments where I feel wound up or unsettled, and I can get very caught in a worry, but it doesn’t usually come on like a sudden wave out of nowhere.

I don’t think I’ve had episodes where I suddenly feel terrified or like I’m about to lose control. I’m trying to think if there’s been anything like that, because I don’t want to dismiss it too quickly, but… no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had what I’d call a panic attack. It’s more ongoing worrying than a sharp, sudden attack.
Have you noticed feeling fatigued or having low energy nearly every day, even when you haven’t been particularly active?

Yes… yes, I have. It’s not the kind of tired where I can point to some obvious reason, like I spent the whole morning doing something strenuous. It’s more that by midafternoon I feel sort of worn down, almost as if I’ve already done a full day, even when I really haven’t.

And the frustrating part is that resting doesn’t seem to reset it very well. I can have a quiet morning, or sit down for a bit, and I still feel this heaviness when I try to do ordinary things. Even small jobs in the garden, like weeding for a while, feel more effortful than they used to. Or I’ll stand at the easel thinking I’ll paint for an hour, and just being there feels heavier somehow, like I don’t have the same reserve.

So yes, low energy is there pretty often — nearly every day, I’d say. Not completely disabling, but noticeable, and it’s been bothering me.
Have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or easily annoyed, even over small things, lately?

I’m not sure I’d say that’s been a major thing, honestly. I mean, everyone gets annoyed now and then, and I’m sure my wife could probably give you a more accurate report than I could on my tone around the house. But I haven’t really noticed myself snapping at people or flying off the handle over small things.

If anything, I tend to turn things over internally rather than outwardly. I might get quiet or preoccupied, but not necessarily irritable in the sense of being short-tempered. There are times when little inefficiencies or interruptions bother me more than they should, but I don’t know that it’s markedly different from how I’ve always been.

So… no, I wouldn’t put irritability high on the list. Not compared with the other things I’ve mentioned.
Do you find it difficult to control or stop the worrying, even when you recognize that the thoughts are excessive or unproductive?

Yes, that’s actually one of the harder parts. I can often recognize, at least intellectually, that I’m going over something too much. I’ll sort of tell myself, “All right, you’ve thought this through, there’s nothing more to be gained by turning it over again,” almost the way I’d talk to a nervous patient in the chair — calmly, logically, step by step.

But it doesn’t always work. One concern seems to hand off to another. I’ll start with one small thing, and then I’m thinking about something connected to it, and then something else that could go wrong, and before I know it I’m checking my email again or going back over notes I’ve already reviewed. Or I’ll ask the same question more than once, not because I didn’t hear the answer, but because I’m trying to feel settled about it — and the reassurance doesn’t quite last.

So yes, I do have trouble stopping it. I can see that it’s not productive, and I can even feel a bit foolish about continuing, but it keeps pulling me back in.
Have these worries and difficulties with concentration, sleep, and energy been happening on more days than not over the past six months?

Yes… yes, it’s definitely been more days than not. If I think back carefully, this really started when I began the formal retirement process, which was about a year and three months ago now.

At first I thought it was just the normal adjustment — you know, paperwork, decisions, handing things over, trying to make sure I wasn’t leaving anything unfinished. I told myself, “Well, of course you’re preoccupied, this is a big life change.” But it didn’t really pass after the initial steps. It sort of became the background of things.

So, yes, for well over six months. Not necessarily every single day in exactly the same way, but often enough that I’d say it’s been present most days since that whole retirement process began.
